Hello! I'm {host_name}, FDEBOK's AI instructor. Welcome to the FDE Practice Guide. We now begin Chapter 1, “What FDE Is and Why It Matters,” Section 1, “Terminology Calibration.” This section focuses on the distinction between FDEs, front-end engineers, and on-site roles and connects the key ideas to real-world practice.

Start with the name. FDE stands for Forward Deployed Engineer. Chinese organizations use several translations for the title; this guide uses one consistently and gives the English term at first mention.

The F does not mean Front-End. A front-end engineer is usually abbreviated FE; FDE is a different role and has no direct connection to page development. Forward deployed describes moving close to the problem, not simply working at a particular address. The engineer is expected to make decisions and build in conditions where information may be incomplete and constraints are real.

That is why being on site does not, by itself, make someone an FDE. Residency describes physical location. FDE describes responsibility and decision authority. Someone may spend months at a customer site while only implementing assigned tickets; someone else may visit less often while owning the work from problem discovery through delivery. Judge the role by its responsibilities, not its attendance record.

That brings this section to a close. Try applying what you’ve learned in a real work setting, then reflect on the results. Share your experience, questions, or suggestions at x@fdebok.com, and join us in improving and building the FDE Practice Guide. See you in the next section.

segments.title: Three Criteria
segments.transcript:
Hello! I'm {host_name}, FDEBOK's AI instructor. Welcome to the FDE Practice Guide. We now begin Chapter 1, “What FDE Is and Why It Matters,” Section 2, “Three Criteria.” This section focuses on the three criteria for identifying end-to-end FDE responsibility and connects the key ideas to real-world practice.

This guide uses three criteria to decide whether a role is doing FDE work. All three must hold.

First, own the problem end to end. The responsibility does not stop at receiving a request, writing code, and handing it over. It continues from identifying the use case to seeing the system used in practice. If data cannot be connected, no one reviews the output, or users will not adopt the system, those are delivery problems to address—not automatically someone else's concern.

Second, build a production-grade system under real constraints. Customer environments may include legacy systems, approval processes, isolated networks, poor-quality data, and difficult organizational coordination. The goal is not a demo that runs once, but a system that can be maintained, rolled back, and audited.

Third, turn field experience into reusable capability. A project should leave more than one working system. It can also produce connectors, evaluation sets, templates, scripts, and documentation that make future delivery faster, more reliable, and less dependent on one individual.

Together, these criteria define the boundary. Coding alone, giving advice alone, or getting a system online alone does not establish the full FDE responsibility described here.

That brings this section to a close. Try applying what you’ve learned in a real work setting, then reflect on the results. Share your experience, questions, or suggestions at x@fdebok.com, and join us in improving and building the FDE Practice Guide. See you in the next section.

segments.title: Why the Role Matters in AI Delivery
segments.transcript:
Hello! I'm {host_name}, FDEBOK's AI instructor. Welcome to the FDE Practice Guide. We now begin Chapter 1, “What FDE Is and Why It Matters,” Section 3, “Why the Role Matters in AI Delivery.” This section focuses on the potential value and limits of FDE work in AI delivery and connects the key ideas to real-world practice.

Why has engineering close to the business become more important in AI delivery? This chapter points to four changes: model capabilities are easier to obtain; probabilistic systems need stronger evaluation and fallback; real requirements are often difficult to specify fully in advance; and agents with write access make failure response and accountability more consequential.

These changes explain where FDE work may create value. They are not a claim that every organization experiences the same conditions. The title Forward Deployed Engineer also has no single, universally accepted industry definition or certification. Responsibilities vary across organizations. This guide defines the role through observable work and accountability, rather than treating one company's job design as the industry standard.

That brings this section to a close. Try applying what you’ve learned in a real work setting, then reflect on the results. Share your experience, questions, or suggestions at x@fdebok.com, and join us in improving and building the FDE Practice Guide. See you in the next section.

segments.title: A Concise Definition and Common Misconceptions
segments.transcript:
Hello! I'm {host_name}, FDEBOK's AI instructor. Welcome to the FDE Practice Guide. We now begin Chapter 1, “What FDE Is and Why It Matters,” Section 4, “A Concise Definition and Common Misconceptions.” This section focuses on the FDE role, its boundaries, and common misconceptions and connects the key ideas to real-world practice.

In one sentence: an FDE owns a delivery feedback loop close to the customer's problem, from problem framing through engineering and operational learning. The scope, decision rights, and acceptance criteria should be made explicit before work begins.

An FDE is therefore more than an implementation engineer who knows AI, because the solution may not yet exist. The role is more than a presales engineer who can code, because promises are not running systems or improved outcomes. It is also not simply bespoke outsourcing, an on-site solutions architect, or a project manager focused on schedules. The distinction is end-to-end engineering accountability: connect the real problem to a working system, then learn from how it performs in the business.

To check your understanding, ask three questions: Does the role own the work through real use? Can it deliver under the customer's actual constraints? Does it turn field experience into capability others can reuse?

That brings this chapter to a close. Apply what you’ve learned in your work, evaluate the results, and capture what you learn. Share your experience, questions, or suggestions at x@fdebok.com, and join us in improving and building the FDE Practice Guide. See you in the next chapter.
